title: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
content:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 6 Nov 2026]
Title:AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
View PDF
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.

report.summary: AlienBench adapts a cognitive-psychology creativity test to score how structurally novel LLM outputs are, finding open-weight models outperform proprietary ones.
report.background: Large language models are increasingly used for creative work such as writing, design, and idea generation, so whether their outputs depart from familiar patterns matters. Novelty is a common creativity measure, but current evaluations often rely on human experts or LLM judges to rate outputs without a fixed reference for what counts as familiar. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology solves this by asking people to imagine an alien creature; departures from Earth-animal traits such as bilateral symmetry or legs provide a measurable baseline. AlienBench adapts that task to LLMs, using alien-creature descriptions and feature-level judgments to quantify structural novelty against a known default.
key_points: AlienBench asks each model to describe alien creatures under six prompt conditions, with 30 descriptions per condition and 180 per model. Three LLM judges extract ten biological features from each description and label each as Earth-typical or a departure. The number of departures, from 0 to 10, becomes the novelty score, and the model's overall score is the mean across descriptions.

The study evaluates 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight systems. Overall scores range from 3.28 for GPT-6 Luna to 6.55 for Ministral 3 14B. Open-weight models average 5.40, higher than proprietary models at 4.58, suggesting that model access type does not straightforwardly predict structural novelty on this task.

Under the baseline prompt, the evaluated models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. That result positions current LLMs as unusually non-Earth-typical in this structured imagination setting, though the benchmark measures departure rather than whether an idea is useful, coherent, or aesthetically successful.

The authors release all prompts, model generations, judge outputs, and scores. This transparency lets other researchers inspect judge behavior, rerun analyses, compare new models, and test whether high novelty scores reflect genuine creative departure or artifacts of prompt framing and automated evaluation.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AlienBench adds a reference-based alternative to subjective creativity ratings, which could make novelty claims more comparable across models and releases. For developers, it offers a diagnostic for creative tasks and prompt design, but also a warning: optimizing only for feature departures may produce strange outputs without improving usefulness or quality. The open-weight advantage may influence model selection for brainstorming and design workflows, while proprietary vendors may face pressure to report such benchmarks. For regular users, the practical effect is likely more visible experimentation with unconventional ideas in writing and design tools, alongside a continuing need to judge coherence, relevance, and taste rather than novelty alone.
report.tools: Follow the AlienBench paper and its released prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores on arXiv; check for a Hugging Face dataset or repository for reproduction. To try the idea, run structured-imagination prompts against open-weight models via Hugging Face Transformers or vLLM, and use LLM-as-judge evaluation frameworks such as Inspect or OpenAI Evals to compare feature departures against the human baseline.
